conflicts.issue: Immediate Adoption vs. Delay of Elected Officials and Boards Social Media Policy (Item 21)
conflicts.summary: Council split 4-3 over whether to immediately adopt an amended social media policy on the floor or refer it back to committee/work session to vet First Amendment and public-records objections raised by the NC Open Government Coalition.
conflicts.side_a_position: Adopt an interim social media policy immediately with floor amendments while scheduling work-session review of external legal critiques.
side_a_arguments: Council had already spent substantial committee time drafting guidelines and needed rules in place right away to prevent council members from posting personal views on official accounts.

Deleting Subsection 3's board content-based restrictions temporarily and incorporating Charlie Reece's Sections 3 and 5 edits mitigated immediate First Amendment concerns while leaving the policy open to Thursday amendments.
conflicts.side_b_position: Delay adoption and refer the policy back to the Procedures Committee or work session before voting.
side_b_arguments: Late addition to the prior work-session agenda deprived residents and open-government advocates of adequate notice and input.

NC Open Government Coalition Director Jonathan Jones raised serious First Amendment, public-records retention ('may' vs. 'shall'), and text-messaging gaps that require City Attorney vetting rather than rushed floor edits.
conflicts.resolution: Don Moffitt's substitute motion (seconded by Cora Cole-McFadden) passed 4-3, adopting the interim policy with floor edits and directing staff review for Thursday's work session.

conflicts.issue: 117 Goodwin Road Rezoning for Eno Animal Hospital (Item 22)
conflicts.summary: Council voted 5-2 to unify 117 Goodwin Road under Rural Residential zoning to enable relocation of Eno Animal Hospital despite opposition from nearby elderly residents.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve unifying the parcel under Rural Residential (RR) zoning.
side_a_arguments: Changing the split RS-20/RR parcel to RR is actually a residential down-zoning matching surrounding parcels rather than commercial rezoning, so it should not trigger commercial tax hikes.
UDO rules prohibit outdoor kennels on lots under two acres, and the clinic plans daytime hours and modern soundproofing.
conflicts.side_b_position: Vote No in deference to neighboring senior residents' concerns.
side_b_arguments: Nearby fixed-income seniors and church members fear increased traffic, noise, and property tax pressure in an established residential community.
Even if taxes may not legally rise from RR down-zoning, residents perceive real harm and deserve deference.
conflicts.resolution: Both the consistency statement and the RR zoning ordinance passed 5-2 with Mayor Bell and Mayor Pro Tem Cole-McFadden voting No.

conflicts.issue: Holloway Street Local Historic District Overlay Expansion (Item 15, X1000003)
conflicts.summary: Council split 4-3 over expanding the Holloway Street Local Historic District overlay onto a seven-year-old 2010 resident petition amid deep neighborhood division over teardowns versus housing affordability and compliance burdens.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the modified Holloway Street Local Historic District overlay expansion (excluding Area 1 and including Areas 2 and 3).
side_a_arguments: Expanding the district provides a one-year demolition delay and thoughtful review to curb speculative teardowns replacing 1,000-sq-ft bungalows with $400,000+ houses.

The neighborhood contains significant early-20th-century historic residential structures meeting UDO criteria, and the seven-year delay since the 2010 petition was a city process failure rather than petitioners' fault.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose imposing the historic district overlay expansion on the petitioned neighborhood.
side_b_arguments: Even at its 2010 peak, petitioners secured signatures from only 26% of acreage and 28% of lots, and a current city survey showed roughly an even split (49-51) with half of original signers gone.

Imposing historic-district Certificate of Appropriateness procedures and fees burdens fixed-income seniors needing repairs or wheelchair ramps and risks accelerating property-value appreciation and gentrification displacement.
conflicts.resolution: Jillian Johnson's motion expanding the district (excluding Area 1 and including Areas 2 and 3) passed 4-3 by voice vote and show of hands.

conflicts.issue: Property Tax Relief Delivery Model: Deferred Liens vs. Direct Grants (Item 41)
conflicts.summary: Council divided 4-3 over whether to assist long-time low-income homeowners facing steep 2016 post-revaluation tax increases through staff's proposed deferred loan program with property liens (covering both Southside and Northeast Central Durham) or via direct, non-repayable grants beginning immediately in Southside while studying citywide expansion.
conflicts.side_a_position: Support immediate direct grants covering 2015-2016 tax increases for Southside homeowners and commission a citywide grant study rather than imposing deferred-loan liens on seniors.
side_a_arguments: Deferred loans place liens on elderly homeowners' homes and discourage participation, whereas modest direct grants keep residents stably housed.
Southside gentrification and city investment triggered sharp assessments that immediate grants can offset while staff designs a broader framework.
conflicts.side_b_position: Adopt the vetted staff deferred-loan program immediately for both Southside and Northeast Central Durham rather than narrowing initial aid or risking unvetted grant legality.
side_b_arguments: Staff worked 10 months to produce a fiscally and legally vetted program covering both NECD and Southside.
Switching to grants without county buy-in leaves NECD residents in limbo and lacks confirmed legal/fiscal vetting.
conflicts.resolution: Substitute grant motion passed 4-3 at 01:12:11.

conflicts.issue: City Cost-Share for Failed Subdivisions: Ravenstone & Stonehill Estates (Item 31)
conflicts.summary: Council split 4-3 over capping lot assessments at $800 for street paving and funding 100% of stormwater repairs (~84.9% overall city share) in the developer-abandoned Ravenstone and Stonehill Estates subdivisions.
conflicts.side_a_position: Cap paving assessments at $800 per lot and cover 100% of stormwater infrastructure remediation because city bond-collection failures left buyers exposed.
side_a_arguments: Residents bought homes relying on city subdivision plat approvals and developer performance bonds that the city failed to call on time.
Middle- and working-class homeowners had already paid substantial HOA/remediation expenses and cannot afford steep special assessments.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose absorbing 100% of HOA stormwater maintenance/repair costs and deep general-fund subsidies beyond standard petition ratios.
side_b_arguments: Using taxpayer funds to pay 100% of private HOA stormwater detention ponds sets an unsustainable precedent not extended to lower-income older neighborhoods lacking infrastructure.
Citywide equity demands spending public stormwater and paving dollars where residents have the greatest need rather than subsidizing newer HOA subdivisions.
conflicts.resolution: Passed 4-3 at 03:33:40.

conflicts.issue: Greenfield Commercial Rezoning & Mixed-Use Integrity: North River Village / Publix (Item 27)
conflicts.summary: Following hours of testimony from hundreds of supporters and opponents, council rejected the 29.8-acre Publix-anchored mixed-use rezoning at Guess and Latta Roads by a 1-6 margin.
conflicts.side_a_position: Oppose rezoning low-density residential greenfields for a suburban shopping center.
side_a_arguments: Separating houses and a 50k-90k sq ft shopping strip with a connector path misuses mixed-use zoning, clashes with the Low-Density Residential FLUM, and lacks a binding site plan.
Requiring new retail to redevelop underutilized North Durham shopping centers is preferable to paving greenfields outside public transit corridors.
conflicts.side_b_position: Approve the proposal to capture immediate grocery investment and economic momentum in northern Durham.
side_b_arguments: Rejecting Publix misses a strong regional retail anchor and economic opportunity long sought by northern Durham residents.
conflicts.resolution: Both consistency statement (05:46:40) and rezoning (05:47:20) failed 1-6.

conflicts.issue: Approval vs. Denial of Proposed Rezoning Near Kimball, Burini, and Cole Mill Roads
conflicts.summary: Council split 1-6 in rejecting a revised rezoning proposal that the Planning Commission had unanimously recommended denying, weighing neighborhood opposition, late developer revisions, and stormwater/grading concerns against the risk of worse by-right RS-20 development.
conflicts.side_a_position: Support the rezoning proposal
side_a_arguments: Voted in favor of the revised development-plan rezoning proposal rather than leaving the site subject to by-right RS-20 development.
conflicts.side_b_position: Deny the rezoning proposal
side_b_arguments: Developer failed to engage neighbors in honest dialogue before receiving a unanimous negative recommendation from the Planning Commission, creating stark last-minute revisions.
Neighborhood residents raised substantial concerns over traffic on Kimball, Burini, and Cole Mill, mass grading, clear-cutting, sound abatement, and stormwater runoff.
As an attractive, growing city, Durham should hold national developers to high community standards rather than accepting inadequate initial proposals.
conflicts.resolution: Motion to approve the rezoning failed 1-6 on a corrected vote after an initial electronic button error.

conflicts.issue: Inclusion of Durham Rescue Mission and Eastern Boundary in Golden Belt Local Historic District
conflicts.summary: Council split 4-3 in approving the consultant-recommended boundaries for the Golden Belt Local Historic District despite petitions from the Durham Rescue Mission seeking exclusion from the eastern side of the district.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the consultant-recommended Golden Belt historic district boundaries
side_a_arguments: Boundaries follow historic maps and full mill-village development patterns identified by MDM Historical Consultants.
Historic district rules govern compatible future exterior construction and would not alter the Durham Rescue Mission's current operations.
No other property owners in the proposed district appeared at the hearing to request exclusion.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose the proposed eastern boundary including the Durham Rescue Mission
side_b_arguments: Property owners should retain freedom over how they use and modify their individual properties.
Concerns raised by the Durham Rescue Mission and Rev. Mills' exclusion petitions warranted opposing the full proposed boundary.
conflicts.resolution: Consultant-recommended boundary passed 4-3, followed by a 7-0 consistency statement vote.

conflicts.issue: City Council Work Session Start Time (1:00 p.m. vs. Evening Schedule)
conflicts.summary: Council divided 5-2 on whether to maintain Thursday work sessions at 1:00 p.m. or move them to the evening to accommodate residents who work standard daytime shifts.
conflicts.side_a_position: Retain 1:00 p.m. Thursday work sessions
side_a_arguments: Monday regular meetings already take place at 7:00 p.m., including public hearings
Daytime work sessions accommodate night-shift and service workers who cannot attend evening meetings
Avoids added staff overtime and multi-hour evening sessions for agenda preparation
conflicts.side_b_position: Move work sessions to evening hours (e.g., 6:00 p.m.) to expand public access
side_b_arguments: Most 9-to-5 workers and neighborhood advocates cannot take off work mid-afternoon to attend work sessions where key policy deliberations occur
conflicts.resolution: Motion to keep 1:00 p.m. start time passed 5-2 (Jillian Johnson and Charlie Reece Nay).

conflicts.issue: Hope Valley Commons Business Park Future Land Use Amendment (A15-0010)
conflicts.summary: Council voted 3-4 against changing 4.5 wooded acres near NC 54 and NC 751 from Office to Commercial to accommodate a mini-storage facility, splitting over South Durham commercial overbuilding versus retail adjacency.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve changing Future Land Use Map from Office to Commercial
side_a_arguments: Staff and Planning Commission (11-2) found Commercial consistent with the adjacent shopping center
conflicts.side_b_position: Reject Future Land Use change from Office to Commercial for self-storage
side_b_arguments: Public testimony raised concerns about South Durham commercial overbuilding and loss of wooded buffer
conflicts.resolution: Comprehensive plan amendment failed 3-4 at 01:08:29; companion rezoning Z15-0023 was continued four cycles.

conflicts.issue: Farrington Mixed Use Rezoning (Z15-0009): Station-Area Density vs. Affordable Housing & Design District Timing
conflicts.summary: Council split 4-3 approving Wood Partners' 500-600 unit Farrington Mixed Use development near the planned Leigh Village transit station, balancing an unprecedented private proffer of 20 affordable units and $1.7M road upgrades against calls to wait for city affordable housing tools and holistic design district zoning.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve Z15-0009 immediately to secure transit-supportive density, $1.7M road improvements, and 20 proffered affordable units
side_a_arguments: Rejection risks the site reverting to by-right RS-20 single-family homes with zero affordable units and zero road improvements
High density around light-rail stops supports FTA ridership criteria while city lacks legal authority under NC law to mandate inclusionary zoning
Wood Partners proffered 20 affordable units (tripling station-area affordable stock) plus $1.7M in NC 54/Farrington upgrades
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose or wait until Durham adopts affordable housing incentive tools and completes Leigh Village compact design district planning
side_b_arguments: Ten units at 60% AMI (plus 10 at 80% AMI) in Phase 2 represents a tiny fraction (~1.7%-3.3%) of 600 units against the city's 15% affordable housing goal
Consultant Karen Lado recommended lowering base density so density bonuses can leverage affordable housing
Leigh Village design district planning had not yet been completed (Planning Commission recommended denial 8-2)
conflicts.resolution: Rezoning Z15-0009 passed 4-3 at 02:12:34; companion consistency statement passed 7-0.

conflicts.issue: Underground Utility Right-of-Way Inspection Cost Recovery Rate (Item 22)
conflicts.summary: Council voted 5-2 to adopt the City Manager's 50% cost-recovery fee compromise for private underground utility and broadband installations, with Don Moffitt and Steve Schewel dissenting in favor of recovering 75% to 100% of inspection costs.
conflicts.side_a_position: Adopt 50% cost-recovery fee structure with 90-day empirical staff time tracking
side_a_arguments: Durham actively recruited broadband providers like Google Fiber and should balance cost recovery with encouraging high-speed infrastructure
90-day staff logging resolves factual disputes with utility companies over actual inspection time before July 1 adjustments
conflicts.side_b_position: Require at least 75% (or up to 100%) recovery of city inspection costs from private utilities
side_b_arguments: Taxpayers should not subsidize 50% of inspection costs generated by private utility construction in public rights-of-way
conflicts.resolution: Ordinance passed 5-2 at 02:25:42 (Don Moffitt and Steve Schewel voting No).

conflicts.issue: Affordable Housing Targets & Design District Timing: Watkins at Weatherspoon (Item 28)
conflicts.summary: Council passed the 300-unit Watkins at Weatherspoon mixed-use rezoning 4-3 (after 6-1 consistency approval) amid sharp debate over whether to approve early transit-oriented density with a $150,000 cash proffer or wait ~9-12 months for the Patterson Place Compact Neighborhood Design District to incentivize Durham's 15% affordable housing goal.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the project now as a vertically integrated mixed-use investment supporting light rail, school/housing proffers, and tax base growth.
side_a_arguments: Developers voluntarily modeled Downtown/Ninth Street Design District guidelines and proffered $150,000 for affordable housing, $15,000 for DPS, and transit assistance without legal compulsion.
With scarce housing bond/tax dollars prioritized for DHA, Jackson Street, DCLT, and CASA, Patterson Place would likely see little city subsidy even after the overlay is complete.
conflicts.side_b_position: Hold individual parcel rezonings in compact neighborhoods until city design rules and affordable housing incentives are finalized.
side_b_arguments: A $150,000 proffer yields roughly 3 units out of 300 (1%), falling far short of Durham's 15% at 60% AMI target within a mile of light rail stations.
Piecemeal rezoning weakens leverage to unify neighborhood design standards across the Patterson Place corridor.
conflicts.resolution: Consistency statement passed 6-1 (Charlie Reece opposed) at 02:50:33; rezoning passed 4-3 by show of hands at 02:51:44.

conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Failed (1-6)

conflicts.issue: Retaining Jordan Lake Stormwater Protections vs. State Statutory Compliance (Item 17)
conflicts.summary: Council defeated 3-4 a staff recommendation to remove Jordan Lake stormwater ordinance language and seek DEQ permit modifications after state legislation placed Jordan Lake rules in abeyance (only Charlie Reece explicitly declared a No vote on the mic during final debate before the un-read 3-4 electronic tally; Steve Schewel, Cora Cole-McFadden, and Don Moffitt expressed support for working with DEQ).
conflicts.side_a_position: Adopt staff's ordinance cleanup and engage the new DEQ administration to obtain a state-compliant NPDES permit avoiding lawsuit risk.
side_a_arguments: Leaving local ordinances in conflict with state law exposes the city to developer litigation and noncompliance penalties.
Engaging new DEQ leadership gives the city another opportunity to return revised ordinance protections later.
conflicts.side_b_position: Reject weakening local stormwater protections immediately while Durham operates under a valid federal permit extending into February 2018.
side_b_arguments: Durham remains shielded by a valid federal permit through early 2018, and wiping out Jordan Lake standards prematurely concedes too much without guaranteed developer lawsuit success.
conflicts.resolution: Staff recommendation failed 3-4 at 01:41:19 (remaining individual electronic votes were not read aloud by the clerk).

conflicts.issue: Proposed Rezoning Near Kimball, Burini, and Cole Mill Roads
conflicts.summary: Council Member Don Moffitt noted state law prohibits requiring conditions beyond RS-20 ordinance minimums without a development plan and warned RS-20 could allow more rooftops or lack stormwater retention and sound walls, yet announced he would vote to deny. Council Member Charlie Reece said this rezoning had consumed more of his time than any issue since taking office in Dec. 2015, criticized the national developer for waiting until after unanimous Planning Commission denial to offer substantial revisions, and weighed Durham's housing supply pressures against holding developers to higher standards. Mayor Pro Tem Cora Cole-McFadden said she listened to neighborhood opposition, and Mayor Bell voiced concern about stormwater runoff costs falling on the city under RS-20 before joining the 6-member majority voting No.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Failed 1-6)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Failed (1-6)

conflicts.issue: Ample Storage Sanding Creek Rezoning and Self-Storage Concentration (4343 Garrett Road)
conflicts.summary: Council divided 6-1 over amending the Future Land Use Map and rezoning 27–28 acres at 4343 Garrett Road to allow a 200,000-square-foot self-storage expansion.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the FLUM amendment and CG(D) rezoning for Ample Storage's expansion.
side_a_arguments: Self-storage generates minimal additional vehicle trips on Garrett Road and provides affordable space for small startup trades and service businesses.

The development plan preserves roughly 14 acres (50% of the site) including stream buffers above ordinance minimums, offers potential transit right-of-way/bus stops, and follows Ample's high-quality brick aesthetic.
The Planning Commission recommended approval unanimously 11-0, and Planning Director Pat Young pledged a December white paper on future self-storage concentration rules.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose converting residentially designated land to Commercial General for additional self-storage.
side_b_arguments: Self-storage facilities generate extensive impervious surface, and roughly eight of the 14 undisturbed acres are already constrained by steep slopes and stream buffers rather than genuinely developable land.
Self-storage is proliferating across southwest Durham while providing very few permanent jobs, low tax yield, and no street-activating retail.
conflicts.resolution: Both the Future Land Use Map amendment and the CG(D) zoning ordinance passed 6-1 (Moffitt voting No), while the consistency statement passed 7-0 after Moffitt switched his consistency vote to Yes.

conflicts.issue: Barbee Road Retail Comprehensive Plan Amendment and Rezoning (Item 19)
conflicts.summary: Council divided 6-1 over rezoning 14+ acres at Barbee Road and NC 54 from Office/RS-20 to Commercial General for a 160,000-sq-ft shopping center.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the commercial rezoning with added design, anti-storage, cross-access, and transit/signal proffers.
side_a_arguments: Downtown/area-wide office land is already over-allocated by >100% for 30 years, and multi-family housing surrounding the intersection makes a walkable neighborhood grocery/retail node logical.

Floor proffers barring self-storage, capping anchor size at 60,000 sq ft across 3+ buildings, adding internal sidewalks and west cross-access, and improving Barbee/Grandale LOS mitigate design and traffic concerns.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose commercial rezoning at the Barbee Road and NC 54 intersection.
side_b_arguments: The applicant failed to make a compelling case that another commercial center is needed near existing retail at Southpoint Mall, NC 55, and Fayetteville Road.
Nearby NC 54 segments (Barbee to Revere Road) already face severe congestion exceeding 110% of LOS D capacity.
conflicts.resolution: Both the consistency statement and consolidated plan amendment/rezoning with proffers passed 6-1 with Charlie Reece dissenting.

conflicts.issue: Voluntary Annexation Requirement vs. Utility-Only Exception for Jacobs Glass (Item 17)
conflicts.summary: Council divided 6-1 over whether to annex LR Jacobs LLC's 9.9-acre Hillsborough Road property along with its new water connection or invoke City Code Sec. 70-129(7) to extend utilities at double out-of-city rates without annexation.
conflicts.side_a_position: Require voluntary annexation alongside the utility extension agreement.
side_a_arguments: The site is immediately contiguous to Durham city limits, posing no service-delivery obstacles that Sec. 70-129(7) was designed to address for remote sites along the I-85 corridor.
Entities seeking city water and sewer utilities—especially when receiving city services like fire and police—should join the municipal tax base.
conflicts.side_b_position: Invoke Sec. 70-129(7) to grant a utility-only exception at double rates without annexing the property.
side_b_arguments: The owner already completed an Orange County site-plan review in 2014–2016 without notice of Durham's annexation trigger and faces an extra six-month delay and lease extension costs.
Durham should avoid annexing property owners against their will when the city already collects double outside-city water/sewer rates.
conflicts.resolution: Council passed the amended utility extension agreement and voluntary annexation 6-1 (Reece voting No) and unanimously approved IL initial zoning 7-0.

conflicts.issue: Measurement Inc. Petition to Remove 21 Parcels from the Downtown Business Improvement District (Item 18)
conflicts.summary: Following a two-hour public hearing under G.S. 160A-538.1(a)(1) pitting Measurement Inc. against Downtown Durham Inc. and downtown stakeholders, Council rejected MI's claim for removal and adjourned without taking action.
conflicts.side_a_position: Decline to remove MI's 21 parcels from the Downtown Business Improvement District.
side_a_arguments: Under G.S. 160A-538.1, Council retains discretion ('may' remove) and MI failed to meet the statutory burden because comparing downtown with BID services to non-BID neighborhoods ignores that the BID produces those clean-and-safe outcomes.
MI directly benefits from downtown's ecosystem, festivals, and $5.25M in city incentives for the Innovation District, and taxpayers cannot selectively opt out of district-wide investments.
conflicts.side_b_position: Statutory removal requested by petitioner Measurement Inc. (no seated council members supported removal).
side_b_arguments: MI's counsel and owners argued MI's 23 on-site security, janitorial, maintenance, and management staff plus private marketing render BID services redundant and other Durham neighborhoods show greater need.
conflicts.resolution: After City Attorney Patrick Baker advised no ordinance vote was required if Council declined removal, Council adjourned 7-0 with MI's parcels remaining in the BID.

conflicts.issue: Process & Financial Clarity Around Fayette Place Purchase (Consent Item)
conflicts.summary: Although council voted 7-0 on the consent agenda approving the Fayette Place purchase, members sharply disagreed on placing a multimillion-dollar land purchase directly onto consent without work-session vetting or redevelopment cost estimates.
conflicts.side_a_position: Support buying Fayette Place immediately to bring the land under public control for future affordable housing.
side_a_arguments: Securing the parcel before private developers acquire it preserves long-term affordable housing leverage near downtown.
conflicts.side_b_position: Support the goal of acquiring Fayette Place but object to bypassing work-session review and lacking clear master-plan and subsidy numbers before voting.
side_b_arguments: Placing major acquisitions directly on consent deprives residents and council of public vetting on full lifecycle costs and opportunity costs.
conflicts.resolution: Approved 7-0 on the consent agenda at 00:43:16; remarks entered for future process accountability.

conflicts.issue: Purchase Price Valuation and Siting for Fire Station 18 Land Acquisition (Item 19)
conflicts.summary: Council voted 6-1 to approve a $700,000 contract to buy ~2.19 acres along Herndon Road for Fire Station 18, with Don Moffitt dissenting over paying above the $600,000 appraised value of five improved lots.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the $700,000 negotiated purchase contract as the only viable site in Fire Station 18's target response area.
side_a_arguments: General Services confirmed the seller would not negotiate below $700,000, was foregoing home-building upside and incurring re-subdivision/sewer costs, and had graded and cleared the site.

Across-the-street Herndon family land is in permanent conservation trust, leaving no alternative sites short of eminent domain, and Fire Station 18 sits at the optimal call-service epicenter with potential county consolidation of Parkwood.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose the $700,000 purchase price as exceeding fair market value.
side_b_arguments: The $600,000 appraisal assumed five finished, buildable lots, whereas the seller is not delivering water, stormwater sand filters/ponds, road paving, or impact fees—creating a substantial premium above net value.
Questioned why a new city fire station is needed near the existing Parkwood station.
conflicts.resolution: Motion to approve the $700,000 acquisition passed 6-1 at 00:44:09 with Don Moffitt voting No.

conflicts.issue: Police Headquarters Complex Construction Manager at Risk GMP Amendment (Balance of Trades) and CIP Amendment
conflicts.summary: Council Member Jillian Johnson pulled Item 13 from the consent agenda to register a dissenting vote against the Police Headquarters Complex GMP amendment with LeChase Construction Services and accompanying CIP amendment, which passed 6-1.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the Police Headquarters GMP balance-of-trades amendment and CIP amendment
side_a_arguments: Proceed with the scheduled construction management at risk package for the Police Headquarters Complex.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose the Police Headquarters GMP and CIP amendment
side_b_arguments: Pulled the item from the consent agenda specifically to cast a separate vote against the Police Headquarters Complex contract amendment.
conflicts.resolution: Approved 6-1 with Jillian Johnson voting Nay.

conflicts.issue: Police Headquarters Complex CMAR GMP Second Amendment (Funding Policing Infrastructure vs. Community Investments)
conflicts.summary: Council voted 6-1 to approve the second construction GMP package with LeChase Construction Services for the Police Headquarters Complex, with Council Member Jillian Johnson voting Nay amid community opposition urging council to halt the project and redirect funds to social infrastructure.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the Police Headquarters Complex CMAR GMP second amendment
side_a_arguments: Proceed with the second construction scope (earthwork, foundations, concrete, structural steel, precast, site logistics) for the approved Police Headquarters Complex.
Staff noted 83% minority/women business participation on package one and committed to providing detailed breakdowns carving out materials.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose the Police Headquarters GMP amendment
side_b_arguments: Public coalition speakers argued the city already spends ~40% of its budget ($60M) on policing and urged halting construction before breaking ground to invest instead in infrastructure, youth centers, affordable housing, and healthcare.
conflicts.resolution: Approved 6-1 with Jillian Johnson voting Nay.

conflicts.issue: Cornwallis Road Property Plan Amendment Denial & Continuance (Items 23 & 24, Pulte Homes)
conflicts.summary: Council voted 6-1 to deny Pulte Homes' Comprehensive Plan amendment for 40.95 acres at 2417 West Cornwallis Road and 6-1 to continue the rezoning, with Don Moffitt dissenting on both votes.
conflicts.side_a_position: Deny the Comprehensive Plan amendment and require stronger transition, tree preservation, and stormwater/floodplain protections
side_a_arguments: Scientists and Duke Forest faculty warned that 70% imperviousness, clear-cutting, and floodplain BMPs threatened Sandy Creek water quality and Duke's $5M upstream restoration
Residents cited steep terrain flooding, Colony Park buffer/lot transition, and US 15-501 bypass ramp safety
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose denial of the plan amendment and oppose continuing the rezoning case
side_b_arguments: Don Moffitt supported allowing the higher-density residential land use transition and opposed repeated continuances requiring neighbors to return
conflicts.resolution: Motion to deny plan amendment passed 6-1 at 02:46:27; rezoning Z15-0031 continued to June 6 on a 6-1 vote at 02:51:54.

conflicts.issue: Straw Valley Mixed Use Rezoning (Z14-033)
conflicts.summary: On Z14-033 at 5441 New Hope Commons Drive, council approved the project 6-1, with Charlie Reece dissenting and Don Moffitt probing whether any affordable housing commitments were legally bound.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve Z14-033 mixed-use rezoning with traffic, transit, and underground parking improvements
side_a_arguments: Halved projected traffic compared to existing entitlements, funded half-signal improvements at Mt. Moriah/New Hope Commons, and received 9-0 Planning Commission endorsement
conflicts.side_b_position: Vote against Z14-033
side_b_arguments: Maintained dissent on station-area rezonings lacking legally committed affordable housing near Patterson Place
conflicts.resolution: Z14-033 passed 6-1 (Charlie Reece voting No) at 02:31:00; consistency statement passed 7-0.

conflicts.issue: Farrington Mixed Use (Z15-0009) Continuance Pending Affordable Housing Strategy
conflicts.summary: Six council members voted to continue Wood Partners' Farrington Mixed Use rezoning until March 21 after the consultant's March 10 affordable housing presentation, while Don Moffitt dissented arguing a delay would not change the by-right alternative.
conflicts.side_a_position: Continue public hearing to March 21 to evaluate Wood Partners' last-minute 20-unit affordable housing proffer alongside the consultant's report
side_a_arguments: Public and advocates had no prior notice of Text Commitment 10 until the hearing night
Waiting past March 10 allows Enterprise Community consultant Karen Lado to advise whether public incentives or more units are feasible
conflicts.side_b_position: Vote immediately rather than continuing
side_b_arguments: On March 21 council will face the exact same choice between this project and RS-20 by-right development; funding gap tools would take until next year
conflicts.resolution: Motion to continue to March 21 passed 6-1 (Don Moffitt voting No).

conflicts.issue: UDO Omnibus Changes 9 (TC15-0001) & Bicycle/Pedestrian Advisory Recommendations
conflicts.summary: Council adopted UDO Omnibus text amendment TC15-0001 6-1, with Don Moffitt dissenting because staff did not adopt BPAC recommendations.
conflicts.side_a_position: Adopt UDO Omnibus 9 technical, historic-district, and affordable-housing intent updates
side_a_arguments: Advances consensus UDO cleanups, lowers historic district petition threshold, and inserts affordable housing and equity intent language
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose omnibus package over omitted BPAC requests
side_b_arguments: As council liaison to the Bicycle and Pedestrian Advisory Commission, Don Moffitt objected that BPAC's reasonable proposals were not incorporated
conflicts.resolution: TC15-0001 passed 6-1 (Don Moffitt voting No); consistency statement passed 7-0.

conflicts.issue: Proposed Elimination of Municipal Primaries in Favor of General Election with Runoff (Item 9)
conflicts.summary: During the continued public hearing on amending Durham's municipal election process, Council members diverged over whether to pursue eliminating the nonpartisan primary to save election costs or preserve the existing primary-and-general system while exploring alternatives such as instant-runoff voting, voter referenda, or true ward elections.
conflicts.side_a_position: Advance administrative documents to study eliminating the municipal primary in favor of a single general election with a majority runoff.
side_a_arguments: Neighboring Raleigh and Chapel Hill use one general election with majority runoffs without voter suppression or disenfranchisement.
Eliminating the primary is estimated to save taxpayers over $100,000 per municipal cycle when primary leaders almost always win the general election.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose eliminating the municipal primary to save money and prioritize voter turnout, voter trust, or alternative reforms (instant-runoff voting, voter referendum, or true ward representation).
side_b_arguments: Bill Bell stated he would never alter election rules to save money; Cora Cole-McFadden described eliminating primaries as voter suppression and urged researching a true ward system and larger council.

Steve Schewel cited Raleigh runoff data (2003 Districts B and D) showing sharp turnout drops in runoffs; Jillian Johnson opposed changing the system now and advocated ranked-choice/instant-runoff voting or a referendum; Charlie Reece supported researching true ward voting and council expansion.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote was taken; Don Moffitt noted that any potential changes should wait until 2019 given 2017 redistricting uncertainty, and the public hearing closed without council direction to return a charter amendment.

conflicts.issue: Delay of Street Closing for Nevada Avenue, Chester Springs Road, and Hickman Avenue (Item 13)
conflicts.summary: Council voted 5-1 to delay the proposed closure of 1,505 linear feet of unopened paper streets for a 14-lot by-right subdivision until February 20, 2017, with Don Moffitt dissenting.
conflicts.side_a_position: Delay consideration for one month until February 20, 2017 so the developer and Tuscaloosa-Lakewood residents can meet.
side_a_arguments: Although the 14-lot subdivision is by-right and met statutory notice rules for immediate abutters, surrounding neighbors felt blindsided and wanted time to discuss stream, stormwater, and open-space concerns.
Steve Schewel noted he anticipated supporting the street closure after a 30-day window for neighbor-developer communication.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose delaying the street closing decision.
side_b_arguments: Don Moffitt questioned whether closing the right-of-way sacrificed street connectivity and a potential connection from Chester Springs Road to Ward Street.
Moffitt also confirmed with planning staff that 27 lots were already platted by right compared to 14 proposed homes, and opposed the delay motion.
conflicts.resolution: Motion to delay consideration until February 20, 2017 passed 5-1 at 00:56:03 with Don Moffitt voting No.

conflicts.issue: Hope Valley Commons Business Park Comprehensive Plan Amendment (A15-0010)
conflicts.summary: Council voted 5-1 to reconsider and then 5-1 to approve changing 4.5 acres at NC 54 and NC 751 from Office to Commercial for a self-storage facility, with Don Moffitt dissenting on both votes before the final 6-0 rezoning.
conflicts.side_a_position: Reconsider and approve changing the Future Land Use Map from Office to Commercial
side_a_arguments: Adjacent parcel is already commercial shopping center and Planning Commission recommended approval 11-2
Applicant addressed concerns raised during the April 4 public hearing
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose reconsideration and Office-to-Commercial FLUM change for self-storage
side_b_arguments: Maintained opposition from April 4 vote against shifting Office land to Commercial mini-storage
conflicts.resolution: Reconsideration and FLUM amendment A15-0010 passed 5-1 (Don Moffitt Nay); companion rezoning Z15-0023 passed 6-0.

conflicts.issue: Alston Avenue & Leigh Village Compact Neighborhood Boundary Updates (Items 34 & 37)
conflicts.summary: Debate centered on displacement risk and appropriate boundaries around planned light-rail stations: Jillian Johnson voted against the Alston Avenue Compact Neighborhood map (4-1), and Don Moffitt unsuccessfully attempted a substitute motion to shrink the Leigh Village boundary.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve Alston Avenue Compact Neighborhood boundaries as recommended (Bell, Davis, Moffitt, Schewel)
side_a_arguments: Aligns transit-corridor future land use designations across station areas ahead of light-rail engineering
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose Alston Avenue map (Johnson) due to community displacement/boundary concerns; separately Moffitt moved to exclude southwestern Leigh Village parcels
side_b_arguments: Speakers raised gentrification and displacement concerns in the Alston Avenue corridor
Don Moffitt sought to keep lower-density suburban parcels west of George King Rd/south of NC 54 out of Leigh Village
conflicts.resolution: Alston Avenue (Item 34) passed 4-1 with Jillian Johnson voting No; Moffitt's Leigh Village substitute died for lack of a second and main motion passed 5-0.

conflicts.issue: Police Headquarters CMAR Contract and FY17 Police Expansion Spending (Items 22 & 29)
conflicts.summary: Community advocates strongly opposed funding a $65M-$71M new police headquarters and 20 new officers during the budget hearing and pulled Item 22; Jillian Johnson voted against the Police Headquarters CMAR contract while the four other seated members approved it 4-1.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve Police Headquarters CMAR demolition and GMP contract
side_a_arguments: Existing police headquarters facility needs replacement as planned in the Capital Improvement Plan
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose Police Headquarters CMAR spending amid community calls to prioritize housing and root-cause investments
side_b_arguments: Over 15 community speakers demanded divestment from police expansion/headquarters in favor of affordable housing, youth programs, and addressing racial profiling
conflicts.resolution: Item 22 passed 4-1 with Jillian Johnson voting No (Charlie Reece and Cora Cole-McFadden excused absent).

conflicts.issue: Police Body-Worn Camera Contract & Draft General Order Policy Safeguards (Item 14)
conflicts.summary: Public advocates (FADE, ACLU-NC, People's Alliance) urged council to reject the $366,738 VieVu camera contract until the DPD General Order ensured transparency and discipline, while Mayor Bell argued purchasing hardware ahead of policy finalization was practical before agreeing to a three-week committee delay.
conflicts.side_a_position: Withhold approving body camera purchase until DPD General Order strengthens transparency, retention, and accountability
side_a_arguments: Policy should require officers to announce recording, bar criminal-file retention of prohibited recordings, cut unflagged infraction retention from 180 to 90 days, explicitly reference discipline policy, allow video subjects to review footage without filing complaints, and formalize public-release oversight
Without accountability safeguards, cameras risk becoming surveillance tools funded via civil asset forfeiture
conflicts.side_b_position: Purchase hardware immediately while city manager/police refine operational General Orders
side_b_arguments: Writing general orders is an administrative/managerial function and DPD committed not to deploy cameras until policy is finalized
Purchasing hardware now allows officer training to proceed without delay
conflicts.resolution: Council unanimously voted 7-0 at 03:42:12 to defer action three weeks to March 7 and assign Reece, Schewel, and Johnson to compile General Order recommendations for the City Manager.

conflicts.issue: Road Connectivity & Donut Holes: 301 Atkins Heights Boulevard Annexation (Item 28)
conflicts.summary: While council members ultimately voted 0-7 to reject the 90-home voluntary annexation, members debated whether straight-zoned residential connectivity via Marchery Road should be rejected outright without a dedicated Fayetteville Road outlet on Atkins Heights Boulevard.
conflicts.side_a_position: Reject funneling 90 single-family homes onto narrow Marchery Road without improving Atkins Heights Boulevard out to Fayetteville Road and avoid creating large unincorporated donut holes.
side_a_arguments: Adding ~900 daily trips solely down Marchery Road without a Fayetteville Road connection threatens emergency vehicle access and burdens an existing 43-home subdivision.
Voluntary annexation creates large unincorporated service donut holes while straight zoning offers no enforceable off-site improvements.
conflicts.side_b_position: Explore whether staff traffic standards considered Marchery Road adequate before concluding straight zoning could not protect neighbors.
side_b_arguments: Ordinance connectivity rules normally favor linking 50-foot public subdivision streets, though straight zoning prevents council from binding the developer to improve Atkins Heights.
conflicts.resolution: Rejected unanimously 0-7 at 02:03:09 after Don Moffitt moved approval with intent to vote against.

conflicts.issue: Paying $2.15M+ Cost Escalations vs. Rescinding Six County Utility Petitions (Item 30)
conflicts.summary: Council debated whether to absorb $2.152 million in NCDOT active-shoring and road reconstruction cost escalations for outside-city county utility petitions ordered in 2007 (including Grand Oaks/Red Coach's failing package plant) or pursue rescission/annexation and NCDOT cost-sharing.
conflicts.side_a_position: Hold the city to its 2007 commitment and absorb the cost increase on behalf of affected homeowners with failing wells and septic systems.
side_a_arguments: Homeowners relied for ten years on city utility orders in making housing decisions; moral fairness requires the city to bear increases caused by NCDOT changes and project delays.
conflicts.side_b_position: Seek NCDOT cost-sharing or waiver relief and study city-tax revenue from potential annexation before committing city taxpayers to pay $2.15M for county parcels.
side_b_arguments: Using city taxpayer funds for non-city residents whose properties do not pay city taxes raises major fiscal equity objections (echoed by Ravenstone HOA).
State transportation mandates caused most of the cost spike, so city and NC Utilities Commission staff should press NCDOT for relief first.
conflicts.resolution: Public hearing held open until August 21 pending August 10 work-session review of NCDOT talks and annexation estimates.

conflicts.issue: Townhome Density, Industrial Adjacency & Adjacent Stream Safety: 1201 Ellis Road (Item 29)
conflicts.summary: Council approved both the FLUM change and PDR 7.870 rezoning for 180 Dan Ryan Builders townhomes by narrow 4-3 show-of-hands margins (names not read aloud) after residents and members questioned density relative to neighbors, industrial buffers, and off-site stream safety along Theodore Lane.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the 180-unit townhome rezoning (4 votes by show of hands; individual names not announced) given staff/Planning Commission support, modest price points (~$160s+), and Ellis/Riddle road improvements.
side_a_arguments: Developer commits to widening Ellis Road to Riddle Road, reserving 61 feet of wooded future River Road ROW along the northern industrial edge, and modern stormwater detention BMPs.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose increasing density to 7.87 units/acre (3 votes by show of hands; members Bell, Cole-McFadden, and Reece voiced questions about stream barriers, buffers, and density) without stronger neighbor protections.
side_b_arguments: Higher density doubles surrounding residential intensity, borders industrial zoning relying only on an unbuilt road ROW as buffer, lacks a TIA despite Riddle/Ellis backups, and puts more children near an unfenced neighbor branch on Theodore Lane.
conflicts.resolution: Plan amendment passed 4-3 at 03:14:44; consistency statement passed 7-0 at 03:15:10; rezoning passed 4-3 at 03:15:59.

conflicts.issue: City Obligation vs. County Cost Subsidy on Six Petitioned Utility Extensions (Item 30)
conflicts.summary: Although council voted unanimously to continue the hearing to June 19 for additional data, members differed over whether Durham city taxpayers should absorb ~$2 million in NCDOT-driven utility cost overruns for non-city subdivisions ordered in 2007.
conflicts.side_a_position: Avoid rescinding 2007 city commitments made to homeowners who have waited ten years on failing septic/well or package-sewer systems.
side_a_arguments: Petitioners voted on city assessments a decade ago and planned their lives around promised utility extensions; sudden rescission penalizes them for state DOT changes and municipal delays.
conflicts.side_b_position: Verify county responsibility, package-plant owner obligations, and per-homeowner subsidy figures before spending up to $2 million in city utility/general funds outside city limits.
side_b_arguments: Other failed-subdivision homeowners in the county do not automatically pay city taxes unless annexed, and state utility/transportation agencies share responsibility for Grand Oaks and NCDOT shoring costs.
conflicts.resolution: Continued unanimously (7-0) at 02:45:01 for work-session analysis and June 19 continuation.

conflicts.issue: DPD Written Consent-Search Policy, Probable Cause & Checkpoints (Q1 Crime Report)
conflicts.summary: During the non-voting Q1 crime briefing, council members questioned Chief C.J. Davis over enforcement disparities, declining documented consent searches alongside persistent warrantless searches, and checkpoint deployment.
conflicts.side_a_position: Scrutinize whether police officers are shifting from written consent searches to undocumented probable-cause searches and whether checkpoints strain community trust.
side_a_arguments: Following council's written consent-search mandate, overall search transparency must not evaporate into discretionary stop-and-search exceptions or unmonitored neighborhood checkpoints.
conflicts.side_b_position: Defend officer adherence to written consent forms while preserving tactical flexibility for traffic enforcement and hot-spot crime abatement.
side_b_arguments: Checkpoints and targeted operations respond to specific neighborhood safety requests and violent crime patterns while following departmental general orders.
conflicts.resolution: Informational report concluded without a formal vote.

conflicts.issue: Historic Farmhouse Preservation vs. Prior Zoning Vesting: Fendol Farms (Item 14)
conflicts.summary: Following testimony from local preservationists seeking to save an 1849 farmhouse on the Fendol Farms tract, Council Member Steve Schewel explored a 30-day deferral while colleagues noted statutory and vested-rights limits before voting unanimously 7-0.
conflicts.side_a_position: Explore a 30-day deferral to encourage the developer and preservationists to negotiate saving or relocating the 1849 farmhouse.
side_a_arguments: A brief pause might prompt creative private preservation solutions before demolition proceeds.
conflicts.side_b_position: Proceed to a vote because prior approved development entitlements left council with only an up-or-down zoning choice without legal authority to compel preservation.
side_b_arguments: Years had passed since initial approval and state law forbids conditioning rezonings on historic preservation beyond voluntary proffers.
conflicts.resolution: Council opted against deferring and passed Item 14 unanimously 7-0 at 01:30:16.

conflicts.issue: Traffic Impact Analysis (TIA) Expiration vs. Master-Plan Vesting Rights (Item 26)
conflicts.summary: Developer attorneys and Planning Commission opponents argued expiring approved TIAs after two to four years unlawfully modifies vested master-plan zonings (such as Bethpage and Davis Park), prompting Don Moffitt and fellow council members to pause and refer staff's revised UDO text back to the Planning Commission.
conflicts.side_a_position: Require updated TIAs and updated mitigation when large master-planned projects stall for many years so current traffic conditions are reflected.
side_a_arguments: Applying uniform TIA expiration rules prevents decade-old traffic assumptions from locking in outdated infrastructure commitments.
conflicts.side_b_position: Return the heavily revised staff text to the Planning Commission rather than risking unlawful alteration of committed development plans.
side_b_arguments: Planning Commission previously denied the earlier draft 5-7 on legal vesting concerns and had not reviewed staff's subsequent edits.
conflicts.resolution: Referred back to staff and Planning Commission 7-0 at 01:40:36.

conflicts.issue: 2201 Angier Avenue $100,000 Neighborhood Revitalization Grant Accountability
conflicts.summary: Jillian Johnson questioned awarding a $100,000 commercial revitalization grant for 2201 Angier Avenue without a committed tenant or legally binding community benefits/local hiring terms, whereas Eddie Davis, Cora Cole-McFadden, and Steve Schewel favored supporting East Durham commercial investment.
conflicts.side_a_position: Withhold support absent a committed tenant and enforceable community benefits/local hiring agreement
side_a_arguments: Public economic development subsidies should include enforceable accountability and local hiring commitments
No tenant had yet signed on to commit to neighborhood hiring
conflicts.side_b_position: Approve the $100,000 revitalization grant based on contractor commitments and OEWD track record
side_b_arguments: Neighborhood residents requested commercial revitalization outside downtown
Owner committed $400,000 private capital with $125,000 toward Durham-based contractors and OEWD could not legally compel private tenant hiring
conflicts.resolution: Item 39 passed at 01:06:12 (exact electronic tally not verbally announced).

conflicts.issue: Item 19: Comprehensive Plan Amendment - Hope Valley Commons Business Park (A15-0010)
conflicts.summary: Motion to change Future Land Use Map at Hope Valley Commons from Office to Commercial failed 3-4.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Failed 3-4)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Failed (3-4)

conflicts.issue: Cornwallis Road Property Rezoning (Z15-0031, Pulte Homes)
conflicts.summary: Neighborhood opponents and experts contested Pulte Homes' 40.95-acre single-family rezoning at 2417 West Cornwallis Road over floodplain stormwater structures, tree clear-cutting, Tanglewood stub-out connectivity, and Colony Park compatibility, while council ultimately defeated the rezoning due to noncompliance with the Comprehensive Plan.
conflicts.side_a_position: Defeat Z15-0031 due to Comprehensive Plan inconsistency, floodplain disturbance, and tree/stormwater impacts
side_a_arguments: Comprehensive Plan amendment A15-0009 was rejected on April 4, making Z15-0031 inconsistent with the Comprehensive Plan under the UDO
Stormwater BMP wetlands should not remove trees from the 100-year floodplain above Sandy Creek
Developers failed to satisfy Colony Park residents on mass grading, density transition, and environmental protections
conflicts.side_b_position: Approve or defer Z15-0031 for infill single-family housing, affordable ownership units, and greenway links
side_b_arguments: Project offered 3.672 units/acre (122 single-family detached homes) as a transition between Colony Park and commercial/US 15-501
Developer proffered five affordable ownership homes at 60% AMI, 50-foot buffer, turn/bike lanes, and greenway trail easements
Applicant requested deferral to evaluate relocating stormwater BMPs outside the floodplain
conflicts.resolution: Motion to approve Z15-0031 was defeated at 02:27:39 (exact electronic tally not verbally announced amid chamber AV issues).

conflicts.issue: FY 2016-17 Police Expansion Spending vs. Community Youth Investments
conflicts.summary: Community speakers challenged funding 20 new police officers and a $65M-$71M police headquarters in the FY 2016-17 budget, calling instead for youth job stipends and restorative justice investments, while council members defended balanced investments.
conflicts.side_a_position: Reject adding 20 police officers and expensive police headquarters construction without addressing racial disparities and youth stipends
side_a_arguments: Public speakers noted disproportionate arrests (including resist/delay/obstruct) and fatal police encounters
Requested reallocating funds toward $2,000-$3,000/month stipends, restorative justice, and neighborhood ambassadors
conflicts.side_b_position: Adopt the FY 2016-17 budget including 20 police positions, police headquarters CIP, dedicated housing penny, and trail investments
side_b_arguments: New officers improve priority-one response times, case clearances, and include a NECD community liaison requested by the Poverty Reduction Initiative
Budget raised dedicated housing funding to a full penny and funded fleet, greenway land acquisition, and retention measures
conflicts.resolution: FY 2016-17 Budget and FY 2017-22 CIP adopted at 02:51:26 (exact tally not verbally announced).

conflicts.issue: Downtown Parking Garage Delivery Timeline vs. Integrating Affordable Housing
conflicts.summary: Staff and Downtown Durham stakeholders urged proceeding immediately with the standalone Morgan Street parking garage procurement, while Mayor Bell and council members questioned why affordable housing over the garage had not been fully evaluated before voting 7-0 to defer two weeks for answers.
conflicts.side_a_position: Explore integrating affordable housing and faster cast-in-place delivery before locking in standalone garage design
side_a_arguments: Developer Mark Anthony argued a cast-in-place deck could finish in 2017 and accommodate ~24 affordable housing units above retail
Unanswered questions remained on income targeting (60% vs 80% AMI), Penny for Housing subsidy, and Durham Community Land Trust management
conflicts.side_b_position: Caution against re-scoping if multi-month legal/RFP delays stall critical downtown parking and divert housing staff
side_b_arguments: Staff estimated researching ownership/rental legalities and releasing a mixed-use RFQ could push procurement to early 2017
Steve Schewel cautioned that staff work on 24 garage units could pull capacity from Liberty Street and other large affordable housing priorities
conflicts.resolution: Council voted 7-0 at 01:57:00 to defer two weeks to allow staff to present feasibility details, staffing tradeoffs, and affected downtown developments.

conflicts.issue: Adopt Amended Social Media Policy for Elected Officials and Appointed Boards (Substitute Motion, Item 21)
conflicts.summary: Don Moffitt offered a substitute motion seconded by Cora Cole-McFadden to adopt the policy with Charlie Reece's edits to Sections 3 and 5, delete Subsection 3's content-based board restrictions flagged as First Amendment risks, and direct staff to review Jonathan Jones's email for Thursday's work session. After a voting-machine glitch, the Mayor and Clerk confirmed the 4-3 tally with Bell, Cole-McFadden, Davis, and Moffitt voting Aye and Johnson, Schewel, and Reece voting No.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Passed 4-3)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Passed (4-3)

conflicts.issue: Expand Holloway Street Local Historic District Overlay Excluding Area 1 and Including Areas 2 and 3 (Item 15)
conflicts.summary: Jillian Johnson moved to expand the Holloway Street Local Historic District as petitioned while excluding Area 1 (601 and 603 N. Queen St.) and including Areas 2 and 3. After debate pitting teardown preservation against neighborhood division, senior compliance burdens, and affordability, the motion passed 4-3 by voice vote and raised-hand check, with Bell, Davis, and Moffitt opposed.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Passed 4-3)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Passed (4-3)

conflicts.issue: Item 41: Property Tax Relief Grant Program (Substitute Motion for Southside Grants & Citywide Study)
conflicts.summary: Main motion to adopt staff's deferred loan program with liens on NECD/Southside homes was superseded by substitute motion adopting Steve Schewel's grant approach.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Passed 4-3)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Passed (4-3)

conflicts.issue: Item 31: Ravenstone & Stonehill Estates Infrastructure Completion & Assessment Cap
conflicts.summary: Split vote over relieving failed-subdivision homeowners vs. subsidizing HOA stormwater maintenance.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Passed 4-3)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Passed (4-3)

conflicts.issue: Item 21: Approve Golden Belt Local Historic District Boundary as Recommended by Consultant
conflicts.summary: Consultant Cynthia De Miranda (MDM Historical Consultants) explained how historic development patterns shaped the proposed eastern boundary. Council Member Steve Schewel moved the consultant-recommended boundary, backed by Don Moffitt, Charlie Reece, and Jillian Johnson, who argued it would not hinder current Rescue Mission operations and noted no other property owners objected. Mayor Bell, Mayor Pro Tem Cora Cole-McFadden, and Council Member Eddie Davis voted No over property-owner freedom and Rescue Mission concerns.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Passed 4-3)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Passed (4-3)

conflicts.issue: Item 22: Zoning Map Change - Farrington Mixed Use (Z15-0009, Wood Partners)
conflicts.summary: Approved rezoning of 19.95 acres at 5708 Farrington Road to MU(D) for 500-600 units, office space, $1.7M road upgrades, and 20 affordable units.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Passed 4-3)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Passed (4-3)

conflicts.issue: Adopt Consistency Statement for 117 Goodwin Road Zoning Map Change (Item 22)
conflicts.summary: Cora Cole-McFadden stated she would vote No out of deference to neighborhood seniors' fears, and Mayor Bell confirmed he also voted No. After correcting voting-machine display confusion, the consistency statement passed 5-2.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Passed 5-2)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Passed (5-2)

conflicts.issue: Adopt Zoning Map Change Ordinance (RR) for 117 Goodwin Road (Item 22)
conflicts.summary: Council adopted the Rural Residential rezoning for 117 Goodwin Road 5-2. When the electronic board misattributed a No vote to Don Moffitt, Moffitt confirmed by show of hands that he voted Yes, with Bill Bell and Cora Cole-McFadden casting the two No votes.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Passed 5-2)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Passed (5-2)

conflicts.issue: Item 28: Watkins at Weatherspoon — Zoning Map Change (3312 Watkins Road)
conflicts.summary: Approves vertically integrated 300-unit mixed-use development near Patterson Place with $150,000 affordable housing proffer.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Passed 4-3)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Passed (4-3)

conflicts.issue: Item 1: Resolution Retaining City Council Work Session Start Time at 1:00 p.m.
conflicts.summary: Cora Cole-McFadden moved to retain 1:00 p.m. Thursday work sessions; Don Moffitt spoke affirming commitment to broad public access across both daytime and evening schedules.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Nov 20, 2017
meetings.executive_summary: The Durham City Council heard the 2017 Third Quarter Crime Report from Police Chief C.J. Davis covering staffing gains (93% sworn), mandatory mental health first aid training for ~535 officers, body-worn camera deployment across 470 cameras, and Council questioning on misdemeanor diversion and use-of-force transparency. All 15 recorded formal votes passed unanimously 7-0, including a bond issuance public hearing for a new parking deck and debt refinancing, consolidated annexations and rezonings for 208 Smallwood Drive (155 townhouses, $10,000 DPS proffer) and Ellis Road Townhouses Phase 2 (110 townhouses), and rezoning for a Durham Rescue Mission bargain center at North Roxboro Street and Bose Drive. Council also voted 7-0 to confirm street-completion assessment rolls for Ravenstone and Stone Hill Estates subdivisions despite resident objections over bankrupt-developer bonds and microsurfacing workmanship, and approved 7-0 an updated City of Durham logo after hearing an alternative citizen design.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Pledge of Allegiance, and Ceremonial Recognitions
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bill Bell called the meeting to order and Troop 405 from St. Matthew's Catholic Church led the Pledge of Allegiance. Audio during the subsequent ceremonial recognitions and consent agenda window (`00:04:47`–`00:29:47`) was largely unintelligible in the transcript prior to the crime report.

agenda_items.title: 2017 Third Quarter Police Crime and Operations Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Police Chief C.J. Davis and Deputy Chief Anthony Marsh reported property crime up 6% (larcenies 57% of Part 1 crime, prompting a Clean Car Campaign), Priority 1 response times averaging 6.12 minutes, 93% sworn staffing, 100% officer completion of 8-hour mental health first aid training, a new McDougald Terrace community engagement unit, and 470 deployed body-worn cameras. Council Members Steve Schewel, Jillian Johnson, Charlie Reece, and Mayor Pro Tem Cora Cole-McFadden questioned staff on 43 youth drug arrests relative to misdemeanor diversion, sexual assault reporting, body-camera complaints/tech glitches, beat realignment, and public use-of-force data disclosure.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing — Installment Finance Contract / Bond Issuance for Parking Deck and Debt Refinancing
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Finance Director David Boyd held the required public hearing on a proposed bond issuance to fund the new downtown parking deck, parking improvements, and debt refinancing. With no public speakers, Council Member Don Moffitt praised Finance staff for maintaining Durham's AAA bond rating, and Council approved the resolution 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation — 208 Smallwood Drive (Catfish Farms LLC)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning Director Pat Young introduced a standardized multi-motion format for planning public hearings, and Planner Jacob Wiggins presented Catfish Farms LLC's request to annex 24 acres at 208 Smallwood Drive (effective Dec. 31, 2017) and rezone from RR to PDR 6.458 for up to 155 townhouses with Page Road turn-lane improvements (Planning Commission 10-0). In response to Council Member Steve Schewel regarding 44 projected new DPS students, applicant attorney Patrick Byker proffered a $10,000 contribution to Durham Public Schools prior to site-plan approval.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation — Ellis Road Townhouses Phase 2 (2725 Ellis Road)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planner Jacob Wiggins presented a request covering ~16.5 acres across seven parcels at 2725 Ellis Road for a utility extension agreement, annexation effective December 31, 2017, FLUM change from low-density to low-medium density residential, and rezoning to PDR 6.678 for up to 110 townhouses (Planning Commission 11-0). Applicant representative Laura Holloman highlighted step-down density transitions and design commitments.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change — DLLT RR / Durham Rescue Mission Bargain Center (N. Roxboro St at Bose Dr)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planner Jacob Wiggins presented a rezoning of ~4 acres across six parcels at North Roxboro Street and Bose Drive to Commercial Neighborhood with a Development Plan (16,000–20,000 sq ft commercial) prohibiting drug stores, convenience stores, gas stations, and drive-thrus while closing Bose Drive (Planning Commission 14-0). Applicant agent Jared Edens explained the site is for a Durham Rescue Mission bargain center with an opaque fence buffer along the Eno River park area, and Bill Judge addressed Steve Schewel's questions on GoTriangle bus-stop review timing.

agenda_items.title: Confirmation of Assessment Roll — Street Completion in Ravenstone Subdivision
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public Works staff Robert Joyner presented the street-completion assessment roll for 233 properties in Ravenstone subdivision, noting objections from seven properties (2.6%) arguing costs should be covered by taxes, HOA dues, or the developer. No public speakers addressed the item, and Council confirmed the assessment roll 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Confirmation of Assessment Roll — Street Completion in Stone Hill Estates Subdivision
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Robert Joyner presented the Stone Hill Estates street-completion assessment roll across 203 properties ($800/lot payable over 10 years at 0% interest, with 22 objections including 15 HOA-owned parcels and one hardship claim). Resident speakers including Vanessa Brown criticized uneven paving, microsurfacing workmanship, and KB Home's bankruptcy without a secured bond; Assistant Public Works Director Tasha Johnson addressed microsurfacing quality, and Council confirmed the roll 7-0 while asking the City Attorney to follow up on HOA quitclaim-deed questions.

agenda_items.title: Updated City of Durham Logo (Pulled from Consent Agenda)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Pulled from the consent agenda for speaker Craig Carter (appearing as a private citizen), who presented an alternative logo concept and argued the staff design omitted key identity elements. Council members praised the thorough staff-led process and voted 7-0 to approve the updated City of Durham logo.

votes.item_title: Resolution Regarding Installment Finance Contract / Parking Deck Bond Issuance (Item 21)
votes.discussion_detail: Following Finance Director David Boyd's presentation and Council Member Don Moffitt's remarks praising the city's AAA bond rating, Council closed the hearing with no speakers and passed the resolution 7-0.

votes.item_title: Adopt Annexation Petition/Ordinance for 208 Smallwood Drive (Item 22)
votes.discussion_detail: First of four standardized motions on the Catfish Farms LLC townhouse project; Council approved the annexation petition 7-0.

votes.item_title: Approve Utility Extension Agreement for 208 Smallwood Drive (Item 22)
votes.discussion_detail: Second motion on Item 22; Council approved the utility extension agreement 7-0.

votes.discussion_detail: Third motion on Item 22; Council adopted the consistency statement 7-0.

votes.discussion_detail: Fourth motion on Item 22 following Patrick Byker's $10,000 DPS student-generation proffer; Council approved rezoning to PDR 6.458 for up to 155 townhouses 7-0.

votes.item_title: Adopt Annexation Ordinance for Ellis Road Townhouses Phase 2 (Item 23)
votes.discussion_detail: First of five motions on Item 23 (2725 Ellis Road); Council approved the annexation ordinance 7-0.

votes.item_title: Approve Utility Extension Agreement for Ellis Road Townhouses Phase 2 (Item 23)
votes.discussion_detail: Second motion on Item 23; Council approved the utility extension agreement 7-0.

votes.item_title: Approve Future Land Use Map Amendment for Ellis Road Townhouses Phase 2 (Item 23)
votes.discussion_detail: Third motion on Item 23; Council approved changing the Future Land Use Map to low-to-medium density residential 7-0.

votes.discussion_detail: Fourth motion on Item 23; Council adopted the consistency statement 7-0.

votes.discussion_detail: Fifth motion on Item 23; Council approved rezoning to PDR 6.678 for up to 110 townhouses 7-0.

votes.discussion_detail: Following applicant Jared Edens' presentation on the Durham Rescue Mission bargain center and bus-stop coordination, Council adopted the consistency statement 7-0.

votes.item_title: Approve Zoning Map Change (CN(D)) for DLLT RR (Item 24)
votes.discussion_detail: Council approved the rezoning request at N. Roxboro Street and Bose Drive 7-0.

votes.discussion_detail: After Robert Joyner noted 7 objections among 233 assessed properties and no speakers appeared at the hearing, Council confirmed the Ravenstone assessment roll 7-0.

votes.discussion_detail: After public testimony regarding KB Home's bankruptcy and microsurfacing workmanship, Council noted the assessment had already been reduced to $800 per lot over 10 years at 0% interest and confirmed the assessment roll 7-0.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Nov 6, 2017
meetings.executive_summary: The Durham City Council opened its November 6, 2017 meeting with recognitions for kinship caregivers, Durham Community Trail Watch volunteers, the late community leader F.E.J. McDonald-Still, and city runners before unanimously approving all five recorded votes 7-0. Council passed the consent agenda 7-0 (including Southside East Phase 2 environmental/construction amendments, Police Headquarters contracts, and Durham Athletic Park operating amendments) and adopted the 2016 Evaluation and Assessment Report (EAR) of the Durham Comprehensive Plan alongside Urban Open Space Plan updates 7-0. Council also approved 7-0 the updated Durham-Morrisville annexation and utility service area boundary agreement and granted project-completion extensions on economic development incentive contracts with Migrate Property II LLC (through September 30, 2018) and A&J Capital LLC (through June 30, 2018), before closing with public comment on gun violence and state preemption.

agenda_items.title: Proclamations and Recognitions (Kinship Care, Trail Watch, F.E.J. McDonald-Still Memorial, Bull City Race)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council issued proclamations and recognitions for grandparents raising grandchildren, Durham Community Trail Watch's five years of trail monitoring, and a memorial resolution for F.E.J. McDonald-Still introduced by Mayor Pro Tem Cora Cole-McFadden. Staff also recognized city participants in the Bull City 5-mile race.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Southside East Phase 2 Amendment, DCHC MPO Study, Sewer Contracts, DAP & Police HQ)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bell read consent headings covering minutes, board appointments, audits, McCormack Baron Salazar's Southside East Phase 2 environmental/construction amendment, a DCHC MPO downtown study, Eastern Outfall/MLK Parkway sewer relocation, installment finance negotiation, the September bid report, the 6th amendment to the Durham Athletic Park operating agreement, Police Headquarters art and equipment contracts, and utility locating services.

agenda_items.title: 2016 Evaluation and Assessment Report (EAR) of the Durham Comprehensive Plan (A1700002)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planner Laura Woods presented the fifth annual Evaluation and Assessment Report rectifying city-county land-use map amendments (17 city and 3 county in 2016) and incorporating Board of County Commissioners-requested updates to the Urban Open Space Plan. Council praised the Urban Open Space Plan, and with no public speakers, adopted the resolution 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Durham-Morrisville Annexation and Utility Service Area Agreement
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planner Grace Smith presented an updated annexation and utility service area agreement with the Town of Morrisville replacing the 1997 agreement that expired October 1, 2017, reflecting updated boundary PINs and approved by Morrisville on October 24. With no public speakers, Council adopted the ordinance and authorized the Mayor to execute the agreement 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Amendment to Economic Development Incentive Agreement — Migrate Property II LLC
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Reginald Jones of the Office of Economic and Workforce Development presented an amendment to the June 6, 2016 incentive agreement under G.S. 158-7.1 extending the project completion deadline to September 30, 2018. In response to the City Manager, Jones explained delays stemmed from replacing the project's engineering firm and additional bank-required brownfield environmental testing, and expressed confidence the project will execute.

agenda_items.title: Second Amendment to Economic Development Incentive Agreement — A&J Capital LLC
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Reginald Jones presented a second amendment to the February 2, 2015 incentive agreement with A&J Capital LLC extending the project completion deadline from December 31, 2017 to June 30, 2018. Jones explained the delay resulted from the untimely death of the project's coordinating architect, and Council approved the extension 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Citizen Remarks on Gun Violence and Local Authority
agenda_items.discussion_summary: A young resident asked Council what steps Durham can take within state law to protect residents from mass shootings and gun violence. Council members shared frustration over daily gun violence and state preemption, and Mayor Bell encouraged sharing proposals with Durham's General Assembly delegation for the city's annual legislative agenda.

votes.item_title: Adopt Resolution Approving 2016 Evaluation and Assessment Report (EAR) of the Durham Comprehensive Plan (Item 8)
votes.discussion_detail: Following Planner Laura Woods' report on 2016 plan amendments and Urban Open Space Plan revisions, Council closed the hearing with no speakers and adopted Attachment A's resolution 7-0.

votes.item_title: Adopt Ordinance and Resolution Authorizing Execution of Durham-Morrisville Annexation Agreement (Item 23)
votes.discussion_detail: With no questions or public speakers, Council approved the ordinance and resolution authorizing the Mayor to execute the updated Morrisville annexation agreement 7-0.

votes.item_title: Approve Amendment to Economic Development Incentive Agreement with Migrate Property II LLC (Item 24)
votes.notes: Transcript ASR renders the entity name as 'my great property to LLC'.
votes.discussion_detail: After Reginald Jones explained the engineering replacement and brownfield testing delays, Council closed the hearing and authorized the City Manager to extend the completion deadline to September 30, 2018 on a 7-0 vote.

votes.discussion_detail: After Reginald Jones explained the delay caused by the architect's death, Council closed the hearing and authorized the City Manager to extend the completion deadline to June 30, 2018 on a 7-0 vote.
